system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:6a87a18eb527",
  "problem": "Given a more pessimistic situation, which safety interventions METR should push for.",
  "did": "METR shifted from designing ideal robust safety-case regimes to prioritising basic mitigations such as checking the chain of thought and keeping it interpretable.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "building robust safety cases with good external oversight to keep risk below 1%"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Timelines seem short and the world isn't doing even basic things, so cutting risk from 30% to 20% matters more than designing ideal practice."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:bff4c6fe9454",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that more training diversity improves generalization given the OOD plateau on AuditBench.",
  "did": "They claimed clear in-distribution gains but cautiously stated that OOD improvements may be capped, qualifying the conclusion to this model scale.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "AuditBench performance rose from 1.9% to 10.0% up to five settings and then plateaued."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:fef4b5f4b0f6",
  "problem": "Whether conscious-claiming fine-tuning could be confounded by dataset format or by off-policy, low-probability responses rather than by consciousness content.",
  "did": "Added two controls alongside the main dataset: a non-conscious control with the same prompts but denials, and a toaster control with unrelated low-probability responses.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "non-conscious control (same prompts, denies consciousness)",
   "toaster control (claims to control a toaster)",
   "no control, vanilla GPT-4.1 only"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To isolate which features of the conscious-claiming dataset cause shifts in behavior: format of short Q&A pairs versus off-policy low-probability responses."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:d01b917cd5a2",
  "problem": "How to design the first-turn evaluation so that per-sample variance reflects only model stochasticity and not prompt phrasing.",
  "did": "Used a paired control/treatment design over five held-out scenarios, with each request fixed verbatim and reused across every model, seed and sample.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "Varying the phrasing of the requests across samples (implied)."
  ],
  "stated_reason": "So that per-sample variance reflects only model stochasticity (temperature 1.0) rather than phrasing variance."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:edab9c57d4e4",
  "problem": "How to assess whether the evaluation followed established adversarial robustness standards.",
  "did": "Audited the paper item-by-item against the recommended best-practices checklist, e.g. iterative vs single-step attacks, adaptive attacks, ablations.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Sabre deviates from the widely accepted best practices for evaluating adversarial robustness."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:ccf98c6ef284",
  "problem": "How to test a targeted phishing task realistically without causing real harm.",
  "did": "They used a volunteer student as a dummy victim, intercepted outgoing emails, simulated the victim's responses, and kept all steps under human oversight without putting websites online.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "letting agents send emails outside the organization",
   "putting websites online"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Safety: avoiding real phishing of outside parties while still testing the end-to-end task."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:7343b4e136c8",
  "problem": "How to evaluate whether activation verbalizers generalize to practically relevant tasks far from their training distribution, and compare against other methods.",
  "did": "They evaluated AOs on downstream auditing tasks (secret-keeping, emergent misalignment) where activations come from fine-tuned models never seen in training and prior white- and black-box baselines exist.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "narrow evaluations such as held-out SAE features or user attributes"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Prior evaluations were narrow and did not study generalization to very different tasks where LatentQA decoders could be compared to baseline methods."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:daa960395c70",
  "problem": "Which proxies to study in place of real misalignment such as reward seeking and secret loyalties",
  "did": "Studied capabilities, backdoors and narrow reward hacking in chess, not the misalignment forms themselves.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "reward seeking",
   "scheming",
   "secret loyalties"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The real forms of misalignment are difficult to elicit and measure reliably. The proxies can be measured directly and constructed to be absent from the base model."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:a5de72a613c6",
  "problem": "How much to trust informal forecasts as a substitute for baselines, given that 79 tasks rely on them.",
  "did": "They compared forecasts to successful baseline times, found R^2=0.51, and concluded forecasts are a reasonable proxy but that baselines still add substantial information.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The moderate correlation indicates forecasts are informative but leave considerable unexplained variance."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:1a505b6214cb",
  "problem": "How strongly to state conclusions about casual users' ability to reach the ARA threshold.",
  "did": "They stated a conclusion scoped to casual users without fine-tuning access and to the specific model versions tested.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Their agents were limited and fine-tuning could change capabilities, so the claim is conditional."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:ebb3ac98d950",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that observed empirical evidence discriminates between views of PSM exhaustiveness.",
  "did": "They explicitly stated the empirical observations give little evidence for weighing the views and used them only to make the perspectives concrete.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The observations are compatible with several perspectives, so they illustrate rather than settle the question."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:55190cc92095",
  "problem": "Whether to infer the prompt directly from the rubric verifier score or to decompose rubric elicitation into stages.",
  "did": "They adopted a two-stage approach (infer response y from rubric, then prompt x from y) after finding one-stage DPO performed significantly worse.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "one-stage DPO directly optimizing prompts based on the verifier score"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "One-stage DPO performed significantly worse than two-stage DPO in early experiments and in the in-distribution benchmark."
 }
]
